title: openssl essentials
summary: Generate a key and a self-signed certificate with openssl, then read any certificate's subject, dates, SANs and fingerprint.

steps.title: Make a key and a self-signed certificate
body: On Linux, macOS, WSL and Git Bash, `openssl` is the tool. Two commands give you a key and a certificate:
# 2. a self-signed certificate for that key, valid 365 days
Or both at once (`-noenc`, formerly `-nodes`, means the key file has no passphrase):
- `-new -x509`: make a certificate, not a signing request
- `-subj "/CN=..."`: the subject, without an interactive prompt (`/O=Dojo/CN=...` for more fields)
- `-addext "subjectAltName=..."`: **the names browsers actually check**; never skip it

steps.prompt: Complete the command that makes a self-signed certificate for `shop.example` from an existing key.
steps.explain: `-addext` adds an extension while creating; `-ext` is the reading flag of `openssl x509`. `-subj` takes slash-separated fields.
hints: Two of the flags are about creation: one starts a new request, one adds an extension.

steps.title: Reading a certificate: the cheat sheet
body: `openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout` plus what you want to see (`-noout` suppresses the Base64 dump):
openssl x509 -in cert.der -inform DER -noout -text      # a binary .cer/.der file

steps.prompt: Match each `openssl x509 -noout` flag to what it prints.
You run `openssl x509 -in mystery.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates`. Is this certificate self-signed? Type `yes` or `no`.
steps.explain: Subject and issuer are identical, which is what a self-signed root looks like (the signature check is what proves it: `openssl verify -CAfile mystery.pem mystery.pem`).

steps.prompt: Chrome shows `NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID` for a certificate made with `-subj "/CN=shop.example"` and nothing else, even though you browse to `https://shop.example`. What did you forget?
options: `-addext "subjectAltName=DNS:shop.example"`: browsers only look at the SAN
steps.explain: Browsers have ignored the Common Name since about 2017. A certificate without a SAN never matches any host, however right the CN is. (An untrusted certificate gives `NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID` instead.)

steps.prompt: This is the .NET equivalent of `-subject -issuer -dates` and `-ext subjectAltName`. What does it print?
code: var root = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Root", null, true, nbYear: 2030, naYear: 2040);
var leaf = DojoCert("CN=shop.example", root, false, "shop.example,www.shop.example", nbYear: 2030, naYear: 2031);
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
steps.explain: `DojoCert` builds a certificate signed by its issuer; its dates are January 1 UTC of the years given.

steps.title: Print the dates like openssl
prompt: Write `string OpensslDates(X509Certificate2 cert)` that returns those two lines joined with `\n` (no trailing newline):
- times in **UTC** (`NotBefore`/`NotAfter` are local, so call `ToUniversalTime()`)
- month as a 3-letter English abbreviation, the day **right-aligned in 2 characters** (`Jan  1`, `Nov 15`), then `HH:mm:ss yyyy GMT`
hints: `{t.Day,2}` pads the day to two characters with a leading space.
template: var dojoA = DojoCert("CN=a.example", null, false, "a.example", nbYear: 2030, naYear: 2035);
var dojoReq = new CertificateRequest("CN=b.example", dojoKey, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
using var dojoB = dojoReq.CreateSelfSigned(new DateTimeOffset(2031, 11, 15, 8, 30, 0, TimeSpan.Zero), new DateTimeOffset(2032, 2, 29, 23, 59, 59, TimeSpan.Zero));
Dojo.Eq("two-digit day, a leap day and a non-midnight time", "notBefore=Nov 15 08:30:00 2031 GMT\nnotAfter=Feb 29 23:59:59 2032 GMT", OpensslDates(dojoB));
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);

steps.title: SHA-256 fingerprint, colon-separated
prompt: `openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256` prints the SHA-256 hash of the certificate's DER bytes as upper-case hex pairs separated by colons:
Write `string Fingerprint(X509Certificate2 cert)` that returns just the `3A:F1:...` part (32 pairs, 95 characters). Hash `cert.RawData` with `SHA256.HashData` yourself.
Use it to compare a certificate you captured from a server against the one you deployed: if the fingerprints match, it is the same certificate.
starter: // hash cert.RawData, then format the bytes
template: Dojo.Check("a different certificate with the same subject has a different fingerprint", Fingerprint(dojoC) != Fingerprint(dojoD), "hash the certificate's bytes, not its subject");
